Entretien avec Francesca Albanese, rappo: Interview with Francesca Albanese, UN special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territories.
Me Francesca Albanese est en tournée can: Francesca Albanese is on a tour of Canada. The United Nations special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the occupied Palestinian territories was passing through Montréal. This Sunday, she gave a talk at the Centre Saint-Pierre. I asked a question and requested an interview for La Converse. It was only late Sunday night that we learned the interview would take place on Monday.
Initialement, Me Albanese devait venir a: Initially, Ms. Albanese was supposed to come to our office for the interview, but because of her many commitments, we had to improvise and bring our equipment to meet her at an intimate talk she was giving at Mémoire d’encrier with a number of students. Many of them were Palestinian, which we didn’t know. If we had, we would have come to this meeting to better understand how Ms. Albanese’s words resonate with these young people. It would have enriched our approach. We did see it after our interview, when she kept talking with the students for a few minutes before leaving for her next talk.
Nous sommes vraiment reconnaissants enve: We are truly grateful to Ms. Albanese’s team for giving us time for this interview. Although conditions were difficult and time was limited, we did our best to structure the conversation around the essential points, knowing that the subject is complex and sensitive. It was a very short window for such a complex subject. I would have liked to have more time with her and more time to prepare.

<strong>Lundi après-midi, une trentaine: On Monday afternoon, about thirty Palestinian students and students from minority backgrounds gathered in the small room of the publishing house Mémoire d’encrier in Montréal. Dressed in keffiyehs, they all had their eyes fixed on the woman they consider one of the most courageous figures on the international stage today: Francesca Albanese, the United Nations special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territories.
« Je suis Palestinien, et on parle souve: “I’m Palestinian, and my family and I talk about you often,” a McGill student told her before thanking her for her work. Between two university talks, Ms. Albanese took questions from La Converse. Interview.
<strong>La Converse: Vous faites le tour: La Converse: You’re making the rounds of Canadian media and universities. Why was it important for you to come to Canada?
Francesca Albanese: Dès le début de mon: Francesca Albanese: From the very start of my mandate, I have been very open to dialogue with all stakeholders, whether Palestinian or Jewish communities around the world, because everyone is affected by what is happening. Since I can’t go to the occupied Palestinian territories, I decided to go to the countries where the demand and the needs are greatest. Jewish and Palestinian groups have been inviting me for a year. Last year it wasn’t possible, but this year I seized the opportunity. I think the moment, the urgency and the ongoing disaster in Gaza make reflection in a country like Canada even more essential than last year, because we are seeing the consequences of the impunity that even Canada helps maintain toward the State of Israel.
C’est pourquoi je rencontre autant de mo: That’s why I’m meeting so many people; I’m accepting invitations from universities where students and academics want to hear me. I have also made myself available to the media and to all interested voices. Unfortunately, I haven’t found much interest on the institutional side, which is disappointing, but that’s the reality. The West refuses to acknowledge what is happening, and today a voice like mine is disruptive, because it carries a revolutionary act that everyone can take part in.
<strong>Vous avez publié, le 1</strong><: On October 1st, you published a report titled “Genocide as Colonial Erasure.” The report broadens your analysis of the violence committed in Gaza and the West Bank, highlighting genocidal intent. Why was it important for you to publish this report at this particular moment?
Je n’avais pas le choix ; il était essen: I had no choice; it was essential to provide a factual account and a legal analysis of the situation in Palestine over the past 12 months. And this situation can’t be called anything other than a genocide. If today we fail to see what is happening to Palestinians as a genocide, it means we haven’t understood what a genocide is. Because a genocide is the destruction of a racial, ethnic, religious or national group through acts of destruction. It’s not only that Gaza has been destroyed – that’s already happened, we can no longer prevent it, but we can prevent the continuation of genocidal acts. We must prevent the expansion of the genocide to other occupied Palestinian territories, to other parts of the Palestinian people. We cannot fail again to identify this, because there is a stated determination, put in place and carried out, to deliberately, intentionally destroy the Palestinian people in Gaza.
<strong>Dans votre dernier rapport, vous: In your latest report, you speak of genocidal intent, which Israeli authorities reject, asserting that the goal is not to eliminate the Palestinian people, but only Hamas. In your view, is there an intent to destroy the Palestinian people?
Ce qui constitue un génocide, selon le d: What constitutes genocide under international law is clear – although it is an insidious crime, difficult to prove, but also difficult to commit. We should have early-warning mechanisms and monitoring systems to be able to prevent it. Genocide is defined in Article 2 of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide. That definition covers acts such as killing members of an identified group, inflicting mental or physical suffering on members of that group, or creating conditions of life that lead to the destruction of that group.
Ce sont ces éléments-là que j’avais déjà: These are the elements that I had already identified as having been committed as early as March. The essential element of genocide is intent, the mens rea, which is not a motive, contrary to what I’ve heard people say: “The Israelis didn’t want to destroy Gaza, they wanted to destroy Hamas, and what happened was just collateral damage. If Palestinians were killed, it’s because they were human shields.” But I think the mistake is to confuse motives with intent. You can have several motives, a billion motives: staying in power, freeing the hostages. But once you undertake a destructive action with its results in mind, you are already on a genocidal path. You are responsible for a genocide because of certain acts and certain omissions.
Et là, ce ne sont pas seulement les acte: And this isn’t only about the government’s actions. In January, the International Court of Justice ordered Israel to investigate and punish acts of incitement to genocide. Nothing was done. Where was parliament? When we’re talking about lethal acts, the infliction of mental and physical suffering, torture, total destruction encouraged by leaders, whether political or religious? Nothing worked. But in fact, it’s not that nothing worked within a state governed by the rule of law; it’s the whole system that supported this destructive act. Gaza has been destroyed. We can’t say it wasn’t intended; they knew what they were doing, and they even explained it: “Take back this land.” Right now, Western legal experts are racking their brains over what constitutes a genocide.
C’est pour cela que je parle de génocide: That’s why I speak of a colonial-type genocide, because people are being killed, a people is being destroyed, in order to take its land – that has always been the objective, and October 7 gave the State of Israel the opportunity to do it, while also exploiting the rage and trauma of Israelis. We have to look at the whole body of acts targeting all the people across the entire territory. We’re talking about acts of torture affecting thousands of Palestinians – it’s not one, two or ten people, but thousands of people, including children. The barbarity against Palestinians. Everything is documented by the soldiers themselves – we should really be ashamed that we didn’t stop all this. To say that these are only war crimes, individual crimes or even, at best, crimes against humanity, and that there is no intent to destroy, is truly “missing the forest for the trees.”
<strong>Le terme de génocide semble diff: The term genocide seems hard to accept as a description of what is currently happening in Gaza and Palestine, as we saw in the reception of your report. Why, in your view, is the term so controversial, when the Canadian government, for example, recognized a few years ago that what the Uyghurs are going through in China is a genocide?
Il y a une barrière idéologique qui empê: There is an ideological barrier that prevents people from understanding this genocide. Beyond the impunity guaranteed to Israel… Let’s be frank: if we had wanted to enforce international law, we have had almost 60 years to do it. For 57 years, Israel has been building settlements, which are in themselves war crimes in the occupied Palestinian territory. Even Israelis, 55 years ago, were already saying: “This will lead to annexation, these will be war crimes.” And little by little, all of this was normalized, not only by Israeli governments but also by the international community. And it’s not just Canada; no one intervened to protect Palestinians where they were, on what little land they had left.
Aujourd’hui, il est difficile de reconna: Today, it is hard to acknowledge that Israel is committing an act of genocide. How is it possible that the state born out of a genocide, the one Europeans inflicted on the Jewish people and other minorities in Europe, could commit one in turn? How can this happen in a state we helped create, as a form of reparation for the Jewish people, and which today has come to commit a genocide? That, I think, is what creates a kind of embarrassment and unease in coming to terms with this reality.
<strong>Et comment interprétez-vous le f: And how do you interpret the fact that you were not invited to an official meeting by the federal government?
Je comprends pourquoi il est bon d’avoir: I understand why it’s convenient to have an excuse not to meet me. Because it will be uncomfortable. Because you have people in power who are, objectively, very competent. It’s not that they don’t know what Israel is doing. But they don’t want to be confronted with reality, because admitting that what is happening in Palestine is monstrous means having to take steps to stop it, and obviously, the government isn’t ready to do that, like other Western governments, for that matter.
<strong>Si vous étiez reçue, quel serait: If you were received, what would your message be to the Canadian government?
Je dirais que le Canada, comme tout pays: I would say that Canada, like any country with a colonial past, has a particular obligation toward the Palestinian people. Unlike the United States, Canada has engaged in a process of acknowledging the wrongs done to Indigenous peoples. If that effort is sincere, Canada must also help other peoples whose existence is threatened by colonial attacks to protect themselves.
Une décision de la Cour internationale d: In June, a decision by the International Court of Justice recognized the total illegality of the Israeli occupation of Gaza, the West Bank and East Jerusalem. It ordered Israel to unconditionally end its military occupation, dismantle its settlements, stop all exploitation of Palestinian resources, provide reparations and facilitate the return of refugees. Given this, what is Canada doing? It has legal obligations – and I’m not asking for acts of solidarity or charity. It has obligations established by international law. Canada has an obligation not to support this illegal occupation. But in this context, what is the meaning of the free trade agreement with Israel? How can we justify the fact that, for years, Canada has allowed products from Israeli settlements to enter its territory?
Aujourd’hui, il n’y a plus d’excuses. On: Today, there are no more excuses. We need to review our political, diplomatic, economic, military and strategic relations with Israel. Otherwise, we risk being complicit with a regime that is committing atrocities. In the past, Canada has had to take a stand, not only politically but also ethically. Whether against apartheid in South Africa – an opposition movement that, incidentally, was born in Quebec – or by refusing to join the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq. Even recently, Canada did not hesitate to take diplomatic measures against India. So this is about consistency and respect for the principles of international law without discrimination. I insist: in a country with a colonial past, this responsibility is even more pressing than in other countries.
<strong>Vous avez proposé de suspendre I: You have proposed suspending Israel from the UN. Do you think that is feasible?
C’était une année particulièrement diffi: It was a particularly difficult year for Palestinians and Israelis, marked by enormous suffering. But the reason I suggested reviewing Israel’s membership in the United Nations is linked to Israel’s actions against the UN itself. The Israeli army has destroyed 70% of United Nations infrastructure in Gaza. Schools, clinics, distribution centres – even when they were sheltering refugees – were struck. Humanitarian convoys were targeted, and United Nations aid was blocked. Israel has killed 237 UN staff members in Gaza alone. Outside Gaza, in Lebanon, Israel has militarily attacked peacekeeping forces.
Israël a également déclaré le secrétaire: Israel has also declared the United Nations secretary general persona non grata and has waged a smear campaign against any UN institution or official who dared to criticize its actions and its army’s operations this year.
Comment peut-on tolérer cela ? Si on ne: How can this be tolerated? If we don’t put an end to these abuses, we set a dangerous precedent, allowing any state to disengage and carry out the same kind of attacks against the United Nations, without fear of consequences.
Pourquoi les autres États devraient-ils: Why should other states respect the United Nations if there are never any consequences when fundamental principles are violated?
<strong>Donc, finalement, ce que vous di: So, in the end, what you’re saying is that, as things stand, the United Nations is losing its relevance?
Mais bien sûr ! Elles perdent de leur au: But of course! It’s losing its authority. It’s becoming less and less relevant in the lives of people who have always seen the United Nations as a means, an institution, a set of mechanisms for keeping the peace. Today, on one side, there are ordinary people like us asking: “What about the United Nations?” and on the other, there are people in the Global South asking: “Does the United Nations only work to sanction countries of the Global South?” What is happening is very dangerous. The risk is that this erosion of international law weakens all of us, because in a world where “Might Makes Right,” we no longer have any means of holding back the force of power. We are in a system without law.
‍<strong>Vous évoquez un système de deux: ‍You describe a double standard between countries of the North and those of the South. In the end, what would it take to compel these countries to comply with the rules of international law?
On ne peut pas continuer de cette façon: We can’t go on this way without destroying the system. It’s not the first time international organizations have failed because they lack the political strength to make the right decisions. What we need is to return to the fundamental principles of international law, to the United Nations Charter, to maintaining peace and stability through the force of law, a law that applies universally and without discrimination to everyone, to the strong and the weak, to the rich and the poor. We are no longer there. Maybe we never were, but now we are truly far from it.
